name: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable
intent: Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist.
problem: Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.
context: Applies when a value has a small, known set of mutually exclusive shapes whose payloads differ, when the same invalid combination keeps being defended against in several places, and when the language can close a set of variants (Rust/Swift enums, sealed hierarchies, discriminated unions) or at least hide constructors. It is equally a boundary discipline: untrusted input is parsed once into a type whose existence already proves it is valid, so no downstream code has to re-validate.
benefits: Illegal states are eliminated by construction instead of being checked: code that would build a value that is paid without a payment date, or loading together with data, does not compile, so the guard cannot be forgotten.
Consumers become total functions: a match over the closed set must handle every case, and adding a case turns every incomplete match into a compile error instead of a silent fall-through.
The model documents itself: the legal shapes and the payload each one carries are the type, so readers no longer have to work out which nullable field matters when.
Validation happens once, at the boundary, and its result is carried by the type (parse, don't validate), so downstream code drops defensive re-checks and stays correct under refactoring.
Tests concentrate on behaviour: whole tables of impossible-combination cases disappear because those inputs can no longer be written down.
tradeoffs: Rigidity by design: adding or removing a variant breaks every consumer. That is the intended alarm, but it is also a scheduling cost in a large codebase and a breaking change for published APIs.
Cardinality growth: one type per legal shape plus the mapping to persistence and wire formats; the mapping is new code that can drift, so the model must be converted explicitly at every edge.

Framework friction: ORMs, serializers, DI containers and mocking libraries often want public no-argument constructors and setters, so persistence-shaped duplicates appear - and their mapping becomes the next place where illegal states are built.

The guarantee is only as strong as the closure of the set: against a set that can grow (an external API, a plugin point) a wildcard arm or a non-exhaustive marker returns, and with it the silent default behaviour the pattern was meant to remove.

Up-front modelling cost and a learning curve: teams used to flag fields must reason about states and transitions before writing code, and the result has more types than the field-based model it replaces.

participants.responsibility: The closed, named enumeration of the legal shapes the value can take; it is the single definition of what 'legal' means and the thing the compiler can check for exhaustiveness.
One alternative of the set, carrying exactly the fields that are meaningful in that shape and nothing else, so state-specific payloads cannot leak into the wrong case.
The only way to obtain a variant: validates or parses the underlying primitives and returns a failure value instead of constructing an illegal one.
Wraps a scalar with its own invariant (Money, EmailAddress, Quantity, OrderId) so a variant's fields cannot hold a value that violates a rule.
Interprets the value through a match/switch that must handle every variant, so a new variant becomes a compile-time error at every use site rather than a silent gap.
Converts untrusted input (rows, JSON, query parameters) into the variant set once, failing fast, so illegal states never exist inside the program.

use_cases: Lifecycle and state machines: orders, payments, subscriptions, bookings and connection states, one variant per state carrying exactly the data that exists in that state.
Client and API request state: a loading/success/error union instead of a data field, an error field and an isLoading flag that can contradict one another.
Message and protocol modelling: a closed set of commands, events or JSON payload shapes decoded once and dispatched with an exhaustive match (event sourcing, interpreters, RPC handlers).
Refined scalars that travel through the model: money with currency, email addresses, quantities with units and identifiers that are parsed once and never re-validated.
Configuration whose combinations are illegal: TLS settings that only apply when TLS is enabled, cursor-based versus offset pagination, mutually exclusive feature flags.
Import and deserialization boundaries: convert untrusted rows, CSV cells, query parameters or JSON into domain types with a failing factory, so invalid input cannot travel further.
Rust's standard `Option`/`Result` enums and exhaustive `match` make presence, absence, success and failure explicit cases that downstream code must handle at compile time (Rust Reference/Book).
Swift enums with associated values and exhaustive `switch` model state-specific payloads such as error cases without nullable companion fields (The Swift Programming Language).

Kotlin sealed classes and interfaces with exhaustive `when` expressions provide a closed hierarchy for finite state machines and error/result models, with the compiler checking that every known case is handled.
avoid_when: The set is genuinely open (third-party plugins, forward-compatible wire formats, protocols you do not own): a closed union breaks on every new case - model the unknown explicitly instead or keep an interface with runtime dispatch.
The data is a plain transfer object that never drives branching: nullable fields on a DTO you only copy around are honest, and extra variants cost more than they save.

The shape is imposed by an external authority (a database schema, generated protobuf, a vendor SDK): consume the generated type at the edge and convert once instead of hand-modelling a second copy that drifts.
A prototype or throwaway script whose rules still change weekly: every rule change becomes a type refactor, and the model may not survive contact with the domain.
The variation lies only in behaviour, not in data: an ordinary interface or strategy is the simpler model; a sum type is for data that differs, not for interchangeable algorithms.
anti_patterns: Struct with a status and a bag of nullable fields: a tag plus per-state optionals whose validity is documented in a comment and kept by convention.
Boolean soup: several booleans (isLoading, isSuccess, isError) whose combinations contradict each other, with the legal ones described in prose.
A tag that lies: a kind field next to a union, an object/any payload or a generic map that nothing ties to the tag (a raw C union, payload: any, Map<String, Object>).
Validation everywhere, guarantee nowhere: the same condition is re-checked at every use site instead of once in the constructor, so one path eventually forgets it.
Silencing the compiler: adding a default or wildcard arm so that a newly added variant compiles everywhere and is handled nowhere.
design_principles: Correctness by construction: make the illegal state impossible to express instead of detecting it later, and let the compiler rather than the reviewer hold the invariant.
Parse, don't validate: turn untrusted input into a proof-carrying type once at the boundary, so the rest of the program operates on values whose validity is a type fact.
Exhaustiveness as a design property: closed variant sets let the compiler prove every case is handled and turn a forgotten case into a compile error.
Encapsulation of invariants: private data plus constructors that refuse to build illegal values, and no public setters that can break a state.
Design for change: a model whose evolution produces visible compile errors is safer than one whose evolution silently changes behaviour.
best_practices: Enumerate the legal states first - a state machine, truth table or explicit list of cases - and derive one type per state carrying only that state's data.
Close the set explicitly (enum, sealed type, private constructor, discriminated union) with all variants in one module, so closure is auditable and enforced by the compiler rather than by comment.
Route every construction through validating factories that return failure (Option, Result, throws) and keep fields private; wrap primitives in refined value types so payloads cannot hold nonsense.
Consume with an exhaustive match and never add a wildcard arm to a closed set; where the set may grow, handle the extra case explicitly and visibly.
Convert at the edges: one parser for untrusted input and one mapper per persistence or wire format, both tested, so a second representation of the state never escapes into the domain.
Test the round-trip through every codec: serialization must reconstruct the same variant, otherwise an illegal state re-enters through the back door.
sources: Minsky, Effective ML (Jane Street, 2010) and Effective ML Revisited (2011) - the origin of the slogan and the connection_state example.
